newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: CLASS ACTION COULD FOLLOW CANBERRA DEMOLITION
People affected by yesterday's implosion of the former Royal Canberra Hospital in which one person died could be entitled to compensation.
A 12-year-old girl died and at least 14 people were injured when the old hospital building implosion sent debris flying across Lake Burley Griffin, and into a crowd of onlookers.
A Coronial investigation, a police inquiry, and an ACT Government-appointed review have been launched to find out what went wrong.
It is likely the demolition company, the explosives firm and the ACT Government would all be defendants in a claim, according to Melbourne Law firm Slater and Gordon.
Lawyer Peter Gordon said given the number of people watching the event, the claim could be large.
"People who were injured in the event yesterday have clearly got a case for compensation," Mr Gordon said.

"We think people who suffered from nervous shock or any kind of psychological damage as a result of witnessing these traumatic events would also have a claim for compensation and indeed it may be that given the numbers of people involved, the appropriate mechanism for progressing that claim is by a class action."
Mr Gordon said people involved should seek legal advice over compensation claims.

"Every person is ultimately entitled to have his or her own claim assessed in accordance with the degree of damage that he or she has suffered...The nature and extent of the injuries suffered by everybody would take some time to work out, but I think it's likely to be a very large claim indeed," he said.

Meanwhile, ACT Chief Minister Kate Carnell will write to all State and Teritory Governments urging a national moratorium on building implosions until investigations into yesterday's tragedy in Canberra are complete.
Mrs Carnell says Australian safety standards for building implosions might have to be urgently reviewed.
ANDERSON ON A MEAT MISSION TO US
Federal Primary Industries Minister John Anderson is confident the United States will accept changes to Australia's meat export inspection procedures.
Mr Anderson leaves today for three days of talks with US officials in Washington on a range of agricultural issues.
US authorities have been concerned Australia's new system allowing meat companies to do their own inspections could affect the quality and safety of meat it imports.
But Mr Anderson said Australia is leading the world to ensure food safety and quality.
"I really am confident that not only are we in tune with the way the world's going, we're in fact leading the way," Mr Anderson said.
"And, of course, the cost reductions to Australian industry if we can secure it, are very substantial, the boost to our competitiveness as a major export industry will also be substantial."
KOALAS WORTH $1.1 BLN IN TOURISM
Federal and state governments are under renewed pressure to protect koala habitats following the release of a study which found koalas are a billion dollar drawcard for international tourists.
The Australia Institute-University of Queensland study estimates koalas were directly responsible for attracting tourists who injected $1.1 billion into the economy last year.
Ann Sharp from the Australian Koala Foundation, which commissioned the study, said legislation is needed to protect koalas.

"They're going to have to start looking at how to preserve this animal long term and that means habitat protection and that's where the hard decisions are because 80 per cent of koalas live on privately owned land," Ms Sharp said.

"If we seriously want them into the future we're going to have to start preserving that habitat because at the moment there's no legislation that adequately protects koala habitats. Koalas are a protected species but their habitat isn't."
VANSTONE WON'T BE DRAWN ON JOBS LEVY

Employment and Training Minister Amanda Vanstone has refused to discuss the merits of an employment levy to stimulate ACTU President Jennie George has floated the idea of a jobs levy, to make big companies take on more young people.
The proposal will be put to the ACTU congress for approval in September.
Senator Vanstone was heckled and jeered as she left an international conference on higher education at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology this morning.
Inside, she delivered an address on universities taking on a global footing in the 21st Century.
Before leaving with a police escort, Senator Vanstone said the levy would not generate jobs, but refused to comment on the issue further.
REITH: UNIONS WANT TO ESCALATE HUNTER DISPUTE
The Federal Industrial Relations Minister has accused ACTU President Jennie George and the mining union of trying to create a national dispute over the strike at the Hunter Valley Number One mine.

Peter Reith said Ms George has failed to criticise a letter sent to Rio Tinto's customers by the CFMEU which he described as a provocative act, calculated to undermine Australia's reputation as a coal supplier.
Mr Reith told ABC Radio he wants to see improved work practices and job creation in Australia's coal industry, but the unions seem more interested in spreading the strike.
"These people in the ACTU and the CFMEU have a track record of trying to provoke national disputation. We've seen it before with Weipa and elsewhere," Mr Reith said.

"They want to run an ideological, philisophical contest when all the company wants to do, and what is in Australia's national interest to happen, is for there to be a significant improvement in work practices in these mines so they've got a future."
REITH TO TAKE AN "OPEN MIND" TO SMALL BUSINESS
The Council of Small Business has called on new Small Business Minister Peter Reith to deliver greater protection to small firms.

The council's Rob Bastian said the recommendations from the recent Fair Trading Inquiry for tighter legislation to protect small business, was the main stumbling block for former Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser, who resigned on Friday.
Mr Prosser's resignation followed weeks of allegations that his business interests were in conflict with his role as Small Business Minister.
Mr Bastian has told ABC Radio, the report into Fair Trading will be the first issue for Mr Reith to face.
POST MORTEM ON FIJIAN FAMILY TOMORROW
A post-mortem examination will be carried out tomorrow on three members of a family who drowned at their north-west Sydney home yesterday.
Police said the coroner will prepare a brief for police on the woman and her two sons, who were found in their backyard pool by ambulance paramedics just after midday.
The woman and her two-year-old son were already dead, the nine-year-old boy died shortly after in Blacktown Hospital.
Police questioned neighbours and the woman's estranged husband yesterday, but did not confirm the cause of death.
Relatives said the woman feared being deported to her native Fiji.
